title: The king's five fires
hookLine: a king asks a proud young scholar five questions he can't answer, and the answer turns out to be the whole cycle of life told as five fires
carry: all of life is an offering

cards: A young man named Shvetaketu comes to the assembly of the Panchalas, where Pravahana Jaivali is king. The king asks: has your father taught you? Yes, sir.
Then do you know where people go when they leave this world? No. How they come back?
No. Why that other world never fills up? No.
Five questions, five blanks. Shvetaketu goes home, stung: you told me you had taught me! His father admits he doesn't know either.

teach.b: Go back to the sacrifice from the first day of this year: a fire, and an offering poured into it. The king says the whole world works like that. Five fires, five offerings.
The first fire is the sky world up there. The gods pour in faith, and out of it comes Soma, the moon.

The second fire is the rain cloud: Soma goes in, and out comes rain. The third is the earth: rain goes in, and out comes food, rice, barley, plants. The fourth is a man: food goes in, and out comes seed.
The fifth is a woman: seed goes in, and out comes an embryo, a child on the way.
Then the line the whole passage rests on: in the fifth offering, the waters come to be called a person. Rain to food to seed to person. And it doesn't stop at birth.
The person lives, dies, and is placed on the funeral fire, the last fire, and the cycle turns again.
Notice who's teaching: a king, a warrior, teaching a priest; the text has the king say this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before. And notice the big idea underneath.

teach.h: ALL OF LIFE IS AN OFFERING.
teach.b: It's yajna, offering, stretched over the whole of life: not only on the altar, but in clouds, soil, bodies and births. It's why fire still stands at the center of Hindu life.
A couple walks around it at their wedding, a family feeds it ghee at a havan, and at the very end, the body itself is given to it.

how: Hindu rites of passage, from conception to cremation, are traditionally performed around a sacred fire, and cremation is treated in Hindu rites as a final offering into the fire.

five sacred fires kept burning on a temple altar
the five fires: sky, cloud, earth, man and woman

games.q: you're Shvetaketu's father, a teacher. your son comes home humiliated by a king's questions you can't answer either. what do you do?
o: tell your son the king was showing off.
go to the king yourself and ask to be taught.
make up answers and send your son back.
games.why: he goes to the king as a student. the king, a warrior, teaches the priest the five fires.

practice: Follow the water with your breath. Breathe in and picture rain falling somewhere far away; then a field, a grain of rice, fed by that rain; then a meal that became part of you.
Then feel yourself sitting here, made, the king would say, of offered rain.

wordCard.voice: Pancagni, the five fires: sky, rain cloud, earth, man and woman, each receiving an offering and giving something new, until the waters become a person.

orig.note: Sanskrit pañcāgni: pañca, five, + agni, fire. the five fires through which the waters pass to become a person.

carryVoice: Keep this one: all of life is an offering. Rain to food to seed to person. Tomorrow, that father and son again. Until then.
